How to pass a Docker build secret without baking it into the image

Short answer: use BuildKit's RUN --mount=type=secret instead of ARG or ENV. Declare the secret once with RUN --mount=type=secret,id=mytoken, read it from /run/secrets/mytoken inside that RUN step only, and pass the value at build time with docker build --secret id=mytoken,src=./mytoken.txt. The file is mounted only for the duration of that instruction and is never written to a layer or the final image config.

Most Dockerfiles that need a build-time credential start like one of these:

ARG NPM_TOKEN
RUN echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}" > .npmrc && npm ci

ENV NPM_TOKEN=abc123
RUN npm ci

Both leave the token recoverable after the build finishes: BuildKit records build-arg values for the build, and an ENV value is written straight into the image's config layer, visible to anyone with access to the image via docker history or docker inspect -- Docker's own "Build secrets" documentation says so directly.

1. Mount the secret only where it is needed

In the Dockerfile, add --mount=type=secret to the one RUN instruction that actually needs the value, and read it from the mount path BuildKit provides (/run/secrets/<id> by default):

RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token \
    NPM_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/npm_token) && \
    echo "//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN}" > .npmrc && \
    npm ci && \
    rm .npmrc

The mount exists only for this RUN instruction. No other layer, no other stage, and no docker history line ever sees it -- there is nothing to redact because nothing was ever written down.

2. Pass the value at build time

Supply the secret from a file (never a shell variable expanded straight into the Dockerfile) when you build:

docker build --secret id=npm_token,src=./npm_token.txt .

Add the source file itself to .dockerignore and .gitignore so it is never sent to the build context or committed by accident -- the mount reads it directly from the host, not from the context.

3. Check your Dockerfile for the instructions this replaces

A secret-looking ENV or ARG default, or a COPY/ADD of a file like .env or .npmrc with a token already in it, is the pattern to replace with the mount above. Paste your Dockerfile into Docker Build Secrets Check to find every instance at once, each with its own remediation, or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status if any high-risk finding remains -- wire it into your own CI to block a newly-added secret-looking ENV or copied credential file before it merges.

Why a bare ARG declaration is still worth fixing

An ARG SIGNING_TOKEN line with no default commits nothing to the Dockerfile itself -- there is no secret text in the file for anyone reading it to see. The risk is what it invites: a caller building the image with docker build --build-arg SIGNING_TOKEN=... hands BuildKit a value it still records for that build, the same exposure as a literal default, just deferred to whoever runs the build rather than whoever wrote the Dockerfile. If an argument is genuinely meant to carry a secret, mount it instead of declaring it as a plain ARG.

DOCKER BUILD SECRETS CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is a secret baked into your Docker image?

An ENV or ARG instruction with a secret-looking name is, per Docker's own "Build secrets" documentation, present in the final image and viewable by anyone with access to it via docker history or docker inspect — whether the value is a literal string or resolved from a build argument. Paste your Dockerfile below and this page finds every instruction that risks that, plus any COPY/ADD of a well-known credential file, with the BuildKit build-secret fix for each.

Nothing is uploaded. The Dockerfile you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own.

1. Paste one or more Dockerfiles

Copy the contents of each Dockerfile (or Dockerfile.* / *.dockerfile) you want checked. Add more blocks for more files — nothing here reads your repository, so pasting is how it sees anything.

Paste at least one Dockerfile above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineInstructionNameStatusFix

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan every Dockerfile under the current directory
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any high-risk finding is found

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a newly-added secret-looking ENV or a copied credential file before it merges.

Common questions

Why is an ENV instruction with a secret-looking name a risk?

Docker's own "Build secrets" documentation states it directly: passing a secret through ARG or ENV "is not recommended, since this data is present in the final image" and can be viewed by anyone with access to it using docker history or docker inspect. That is true whether the ENV value is a literal string in the Dockerfile or resolved from a build argument (ARG TOKEN, then ENV TOKEN=$TOKEN) — either way, the resolved value is written into the image's config layer and stays there even if a later instruction deletes the file it came from.

Does this tool verify that a flagged name actually holds a secret?

No, and it cannot. This is a name-pattern heuristic over Dockerfile text, not a value scanner — it never sees what a build actually resolves ARG or ENV to. A name like API_KEY is flagged because it looks like a secret, even if the value behind it is a public, non-sensitive identifier; a genuine secret under an unrecognised name is a false negative this tool cannot close. Read every finding and use your own judgment.

What is the difference between the three finding types?

env-secret and sensitive-copy are flagged unconditionally: an ENV value is always baked into the image config, and a copied credential file persists in its layer even after a later instruction deletes it. arg-literal means a secret-looking ARG carries a default value written directly in the Dockerfile — committed to source control. arg-declared is advisory only: a bare ARG with no default commits nothing to the Dockerfile itself, but invites a caller to pass a secret with --build-arg, which BuildKit still records for the build unless it is mounted as a build secret instead.

Does this tool fetch or send anything anywhere?

No. It makes no network calls of any kind — nothing here can, because nothing here talks to a registry, a secrets manager, or any API. The Dockerfile text you paste is read entirely in this browser tab and never leaves your device.

More: how to pass a Docker build secret without baking it into the image. Already run gitleaks? See how this checker compares for the Dockerfile-instruction question specifically, or see how it compares to reading a Dockerfile by hand.

A build-time secret is one slice of a hardened container pipeline: Docker Base Image Pin Check asks whether the base image your FROM line starts from is addressed immutably, Terraform Plan Secret Exposure Check and GitHub Actions Secret Leak Check ask the same "is a secret about to be exposed" question of a Terraform plan and a CI workflow, respectively, and Git Exposure Checker asks it of a deployed webroot's own .git directory -- a publicly readable one lets anyone reconstruct the full commit history, including a secret this checker would have caught before a later commit removed it from the working tree. vs-gitleaks.html.text:
← Docker Build Secrets Check

Docker Build Secrets Check vs. gitleaks

Related tools, different jobs. gitleaks is a general secret scanner: regex and entropy over tracked files, with no idea that a Dockerfile ENV always bakes its resolved value into the image config regardless of that value's shape. This page checks the Dockerfile-instruction question directly, free, in your browser, with no install.

What each tool is for

gitleaks (github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks) is an open-source secret scanner that, per its own public documentation, walks a git repository's history and working tree (or an arbitrary directory) looking for values matching a configurable set of regex and entropy rules, across every file type it is pointed at -- not specific to Dockerfiles or any other single format. It runs as a CLI, a pre-commit hook, or a CI action.

This checker does one narrower thing: you paste the text of a Dockerfile, and it lists every ENV or ARG instruction whose name looks like a secret, and every COPY/ADD naming a well-known credential file (.env, id_rsa, .npmrc, .aws/credentials, ...) -- with the exact BuildKit --mount=type=secret fix for each. It understands what a Dockerfile instruction actually does: an ENV NAME=$ARG_REF line carries no literal secret text for a regex to match, and a bare ARG SIGNING_TOKEN declaration has no value in the file at all, yet both are flagged here because the risk is in what the instruction does at build time, not in what the line looks like. It runs entirely in your browser, needs no install, and makes no network call of its own.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
Does my whole repository, across its full git history, contain any secret-shaped string in any file?gitleaks -- that is its entire job, and this tool does not attempt any of it.
Does my Dockerfile bake a secret into the image via ENV or a literal ARG default, or copy in a credential file, regardless of whether that value is literal text a regex could match?This checker -- a file:line list of the specific Dockerfile instructions at risk, with a BuildKit fix for each.
My Dockerfile has ARG SIGNING_TOKEN with no default at all -- is that a risk?Only this checker flags it: there is no secret-shaped text on that line for a regex scanner to match, but the bare declaration still invites an unsafe --build-arg at build time.
I want this wired into CI to block a merge automatically.Either: gitleaks' own CI integration for repository-wide secret scanning, or this tool's check.py --fail-on-risk for the Dockerfile-instruction question specifically.

The two are complementary, not competing: a repository can run gitleaks for the broad, repository-wide scan it is built for and still reach for this tool for the Dockerfile-instruction question gitleaks has no way to ask.

Run the free build secrets check

Common questions

Should I use this checker or gitleaks?

Different shapes of tool for a related but different question. gitleaks is a general-purpose secret scanner -- per its own public documentation, it walks a git repository's history and working tree (or an arbitrary directory) looking for values that match a configurable set of regex and entropy rules, across every file type, not just Dockerfiles. This tool checks Dockerfile instructions specifically: whether an ENV or ARG name looks like a secret, and whether a COPY or ADD names a well-known credential file, regardless of whether the value behind that name is present in any git-tracked file at all. If you want broad secret detection across an entire codebase and its history, gitleaks is built for exactly that and this tool does not attempt it. If you want the specific answer to "does this Dockerfile bake a secret into docker inspect, or copy a credential file into a layer," this is the narrower, Dockerfile-aware tool for that question.

Wouldn't gitleaks already catch a secret in a Dockerfile?

Only the shapes its regex and entropy rules are built to catch, and only where it looks. A literal high-entropy value in a Dockerfile line, like ARG API_KEY=sk_live_abc123..., is exactly the kind of value gitleaks' rules are designed to find. What a general text scanner has no way to know, because it is not aware of Dockerfile instruction semantics, is that an ENV instruction bakes its resolved value into the image's config layer regardless of the value's shape -- a value assigned from a build argument (ENV TOKEN=$TOKEN) carries no literal secret text in the Dockerfile line itself for a regex to match, and a bare ARG SIGNING_TOKEN declaration with no default has no value in the file at all, yet both are real exposure risks this tool flags specifically because it understands what each Dockerfile instruction does. And a secret scanner walking a git repository has nothing to scan if the credential file a COPY instruction names, such as a local .aws/credentials, is itself untracked or gitignored -- present on disk, absent from the history a repo-scanner reads.

Why would I need a separate checker if gitleaks already exists?

Two reasons. First, the coverage gap above: gitleaks looks for secret-shaped text, and this tool's entire reason to exist is the instruction-level question a text scan cannot ask -- does this ENV or ARG bake a value into the image regardless of its shape, and does this COPY name a credential file regardless of whether that file's contents are scannable at all. Second, gitleaks is a Go binary you install and run against a repository; this tool is also available as a page you open with nothing to install, for a quick check on a single Dockerfile you have not wired into a scanner yet. Neither point is a criticism of gitleaks' own scope -- general secret scanning across an entire codebase is a different, and broader, job than this tool attempts, which is exactly why a narrower, Dockerfile-aware check is worth having alongside it.

Is this page affiliated with gitleaks?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the gitleaks project or its maintainers. gitleaks is an open-source secret scanner, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using facts drawn from its own public documentation and source repository at github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks.

vs-reading-a-dockerfile-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to Docker Build Secrets Check

Docker Build Secrets Check vs. reading a Dockerfile by hand

Skimming a Dockerfile for an obvious ARG DB_PASSWORD=hunter2 genuinely works, and it is the method most people already use. This page names no product or company being compared against: "reading the Dockerfile by hand" is a generic manual habit, not a competing tool.

CaseReading the Dockerfile by handThis tool
A literal secret-looking default, ARG DB_PASSWORD=hunter2Correctly caught by a reviewer who knows to look for itCorrectly caught the same way, as arg-literal
An ENV value resolved from a build argument, ENV API_KEY=$API_KEYNo literal secret text on the line to react to -- easy to read as cleanFlags the ENV variable's name against a secret-pattern list regardless of where its value comes from
A bare ARG SIGNING_TOKEN with no default at allReads as the safe version of the pattern already being watched for -- no value is visible to object toFlags it as an advisory-only arg-declared finding, since it still invites an unsafe --build-arg
A COPY .env /app/.env among a dozen ordinary COPY linesEasy to miss without checking every source path against a credential-filename listChecks every COPY/ADD source's basename and path against that fixed list every time
Checking every Dockerfile in a repository on every dependency-bump PRManual, and the first thing skipped under time pressureCLI scans a whole checkout in one pass; --fail-on-risk blocks CI

The gap that matters most: a value with no literal text to see

ENV TOKEN=$TOKEN and a bare ARG SIGNING_TOKEN both carry no secret-shaped string anywhere in the Dockerfile for a reviewer to react to -- there is nothing that looks wrong on the line itself. But per Docker's own "Build secrets" documentation, an ENV instruction's resolved value is written into the image's config layer regardless of where that value came from, and a bare ARG still invites a caller to pass a secret with --build-arg, which BuildKit records for the build unless it is mounted as a build secret instead. This tool checks the instruction and the variable's name, not whether a literal value is visible in the file, so both cases are flagged the same as a line with a literal default would be.

The gap that matters second: a credential file among ordinary COPY lines

A typical Dockerfile has several ordinary COPY instructions in a row -- package.json, source directories, config files -- and a COPY .env /app/.env or COPY id_rsa /root/.ssh/id_rsa reads no differently from any of them on a skim unless a reviewer is deliberately checking each source's basename against a list of well-known credential filenames. This tool checks every COPY/ADD source against that fixed list every time, so the answer does not depend on a reviewer's memory of which filenames count.

When to still read the Dockerfile yourself

This is a name-pattern heuristic, not a value scanner -- it never sees what a build actually resolves ARG or ENV to, so a name like API_KEY is flagged whether or not the value behind it is sensitive, and a genuine secret under a name this tool's pattern list does not recognise is a false negative it cannot close. Deciding whether a specific flagged instruction is a real exposure, and catching a secret under an unrecognised name, is still a job for reading the Dockerfile yourself.

Common questions

What does reading a Dockerfile by hand actually catch?

A reviewer who knows to look can spot the obvious case immediately: an ARG or ENV line with a literal-looking secret value sitting right there in the text, such as ARG DB_PASSWORD=hunter2. That review genuinely works when the value is literal and the line is short -- the same case this tool's classify.mjs also flags as arg-literal or env-secret.

Why does an ENV value resolved from a build argument slip past a skim?

ENV NODE_ENV=production API_KEY=$API_KEY carries no literal secret text on that line for a reviewer to react to -- the value only exists once the build resolves the ARG reference. But per Docker's own documentation, whatever that value resolves to is written into the image's config layer exactly the same as a literal would be, and stays there. A reviewer scanning for a suspicious-looking string has nothing to see on this line; this tool flags it because it checks the ENV variable's name against a secret-pattern list, not the literal text of its value.

Why is a bare ARG with no default easy to wave through?

ARG SIGNING_TOKEN with no default commits nothing to the Dockerfile itself, so on a skim it looks like the safe version of the ARG PASSWORD=hunter2 pattern a reviewer already knows to flag. It is still worth a second look: it invites a caller to pass a value with --build-arg, which BuildKit still records for the build unless that value is mounted as a build secret instead. This tool flags it too, as an advisory-only arg-declared finding, so it does not get silently classed as fine because it has no visible value.

Why is a COPY of a credential file easy to miss among ordinary COPY lines?

A Dockerfile can carry a dozen ordinary COPY instructions -- package.json, source directories, config files -- and a COPY .env /app/.env or COPY id_rsa /root/.ssh/id_rsa reads the same at a glance as any of them unless a reviewer is specifically checking each source path against a list of well-known credential filenames (.env, id_rsa, .npmrc, .aws/credentials, and others). That list is easy to not have fully in mind while reading past several ordinary-looking COPY lines in a row. This tool checks every COPY and ADD source's basename and path against that fixed list every time, regardless of how many other COPY lines surround it.

Does this replace understanding whether a flagged name actually holds a secret?

No. This is a name-pattern heuristic over Dockerfile text, not a value scanner -- it never sees what a build actually resolves ARG or ENV to, so a name like API_KEY is flagged because it looks like a secret even if the value behind it is not sensitive. Deciding whether a specific flagged instruction is a real exposure, and catching a secret under a name this tool's pattern list does not recognise, is still a job for reading the Dockerfile yourself.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks Dockerfile instructions by name pattern. A clean report describes what that check found, not a guarantee your build has no secret exposure generally.
